nodes.label: Aortic valve
nodes.summary: Usually three-cusp valve between the left ventricle and the aorta. It opens in systole and closes at the start of diastole, producing the aortic part of S2.

nodes.label: Coronary arteries
nodes.summary: The left main (dividing into the LAD and circumflex) and the right coronary artery supply the heart muscle. They fill mainly in diastole, so a fast heart rate or low diastolic pressure cuts myocardial oxygen supply.

nodes.label: Left atrium
nodes.summary: Receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and passes it through the mitral valve to the left ventricle. When the mitral valve leaks or the LV stiffens, pressure here backs up into the lungs.

nodes.label: Left ventricle
nodes.summary: Thick-walled chamber that pumps oxygenated blood through the aortic valve into the aorta. Its function sets cardiac output and is the main target of inotropes and LV support devices.

nodes.label: Mitral valve
nodes.summary: Two-leaflet valve between the left atrium and left ventricle. It closes at the start of systole (part of S1) and is held shut by the chordae tendineae and papillary muscles.

nodes.label: Papillary muscles
nodes.summary: Muscles in the left ventricular wall that anchor the mitral leaflets through the chordae tendineae, so the valve cannot flip back into the atrium in systole. The posteromedial muscle usually has a single coronary blood supply, which makes it more likely to rupture after MI.

nodes.label: Acute mitral regurgitation
nodes.summary: A sudden leak of the mitral valve, for example from papillary muscle rupture after MI, chordal rupture or endocarditis. The left atrium has no time to enlarge, so pressure surges into the lungs and forward output drops.

levers.why: The leaked volume returns to the LV each beat, raising LV and left atrial filling pressures.

nursingPriorities: Watch for sudden dyspnea, crackles, pink frothy sputum and falling SpO2, and escalate immediately.
After an MI, a new murmur or sudden pulmonary edema calls for urgent echo and surgical consult.
Monitor BP closely during afterload reduction; vasodilators need an adequate MAP.

nodes.label: Aortic stenosis
nodes.summary: Narrowing of the aortic valve opening, most often from age-related calcification or a bicuspid valve. The LV must generate higher pressure to eject, so it thickens. Once symptoms start, outcomes without valve replacement are poor.

levers.why: The narrowed valve is a fixed obstruction, so the LV must push against a higher pressure.
Higher wall stress and a thickened LV raise myocardial oxygen demand, so angina can occur even with normal coronaries.

nursingPriorities: Treat as preload-dependent: avoid sudden drops in preload, such as rapid diuresis or nitrates, without a provider plan, and report hypotension early.
Report new exertional chest pain, syncope or dyspnea; symptom onset marks severe disease and triggers valve replacement review.
New atrial fibrillation or tachycardia is poorly tolerated, because the stiff LV relies on atrial kick and diastolic filling time; report it promptly.

nodes.label: Cardiogenic shock
nodes.summary: A low cardiac output state from heart dysfunction that causes tissue hypoperfusion, most often after acute MI. The SCAI scale stages it from A (at risk) to E (extremis) so teams can escalate early.

levers.why: Loss of working LV muscle, most often from MI, lowers stroke volume.
Hypotension lowers coronary perfusion pressure, which worsens ischemia in a downward spiral.

nursingPriorities: Trend MAP, lactate, urine output, mental status and skin perfusion together; one normal value does not prove adequate perfusion.
Escalate early: SCAI stage B (hypotension or tachycardia without hypoperfusion) is the window before lactate rises.
After MI with shock, prepare for emergency transfer to the cath lab.

nodes.label: Exertional angina, syncope and dyspnea
nodes.summary: The classic symptoms of severe aortic stenosis, usually appearing first with exertion. Their onset is a key trigger for valve replacement.

nodes.label: Cool, mottled extremities
nodes.summary: Cool, clammy or mottled skin and slow capillary refill from vasoconstriction as the body diverts blood to vital organs.

nodes.label: Crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur
nodes.summary: Harsh systolic ejection murmur loudest at the right upper sternal border, often radiating to the carotids. A later peak and a soft or absent S2 suggest more severe stenosis.

nodes.label: Echo: aortic valve area and gradient
nodes.summary: Severe aortic stenosis on echo is typically a valve area of 1.0 cm2 or less, a peak velocity of 4 m/s or more, or a mean gradient of 40 mmHg or more.

nodes.label: Elevated lactate
nodes.summary: Blood lactate of 2 mmol/L or more reflects tissue hypoperfusion in shock. A rising or non-clearing lactate signals worsening shock.

nodes.label: Flash pulmonary edema
nodes.summary: Sudden fluid in the lungs from a rapid rise in left atrial pressure: severe dyspnea, crackles, hypoxemia and sometimes pink frothy sputum.

nodes.label: Holosystolic apical murmur
nodes.summary: A blowing murmur through all of systole, loudest at the apex and radiating to the left axilla. In acute mitral regurgitation it may be short or soft, so a quiet murmur does not rule it out.

nodes.label: Low cardiac index
nodes.summary: Classic hemodynamic criteria for cardiogenic shock include a cardiac index below 1.8 L/min/m2 without support (or 2.2 with support) and a wedge pressure above 15 mmHg, measured by pulmonary artery catheter.

nodes.label: Low SvO2 or ScvO2
nodes.summary: Low mixed venous (SvO2) or central venous (ScvO2) oxygen saturation means tissues are extracting more oxygen because delivery is low. Normal SvO2 is about 60 to 80 percent.

nodes.label: Low urine output
nodes.summary: Urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/h shows reduced kidney perfusion. In shock it is an early sign, tracked hourly.

nodes.label: Pulsus parvus et tardus
nodes.summary: A weak (parvus) and late-peaking (tardus) carotid pulse caused by slow ejection through a narrowed aortic valve.

nodes.label: Dobutamine
nodes.summary: Inotrope acting mainly on beta-1 receptors. It raises contractility and heart rate, and can lower blood pressure through mild beta-2 vasodilation.

levers.why: Beta-1 stimulation strengthens each contraction.
Beta-1 stimulation also speeds the heart rate.
More work per beat and per minute raises myocardial oxygen demand.

nursingPriorities: Watch for tachycardia, new arrhythmias and hypotension; dobutamine does not raise BP by itself.
Expect it to be paired with a vasopressor when MAP is low, per orders.

nodes.label: Furosemide
nodes.summary: Loop diuretic that blocks sodium reabsorption in the loop of Henle. It removes volume and lowers filling pressures in congestion.

levers.why: Volume removal lowers ventricular filling pressure and pulmonary congestion.

nursingPriorities: Track intake and output, daily weight, potassium, magnesium and creatinine.
Watch for hypotension, especially in preload-dependent patients such as those with severe aortic stenosis.

nodes.label: Milrinone
nodes.summary: Phosphodiesterase-3 inhibitor that raises contractility and dilates blood vessels, an inodilator. It is cleared by the kidneys and has a longer half-life than dobutamine.

levers.why: Higher intracellular cAMP strengthens contraction.
Vasodilation lowers systemic vascular resistance.

nursingPriorities: Expect hypotension, especially with a loading dose; watch MAP closely.
It accumulates in kidney dysfunction, so trend creatinine and urine output and confirm renal dosing.
Monitor telemetry for arrhythmias.

nodes.label: Sodium nitroprusside
nodes.summary: Fast-acting, short half-life vasodilator of arteries and veins. It lowers afterload and preload and is titrated minute to minute, usually with an arterial line.

levers.why: Arterial dilation lowers the pressure the LV ejects against.
Venous dilation lowers return to the heart.

nursingPriorities: Use continuous arterial BP monitoring and titrate exactly per order.
Protect from light per the label, and watch for cyanide or thiocyanate toxicity with high doses, long infusions, or kidney or liver dysfunction.

nodes.label: Norepinephrine
nodes.summary: Vasopressor with strong alpha-1 and some beta-1 effect. It is the commonly preferred first-line vasopressor in cardiogenic shock.

levers.why: Alpha-1 vasoconstriction raises systemic vascular resistance and MAP.
Modest beta-1 stimulation adds some inotropy.
A higher diastolic pressure supports coronary perfusion.

nursingPriorities: Infuse through a central line when possible; for peripheral use follow the facility protocol and check the site often for extravasation.
Titrate to the ordered MAP target, and watch for arrhythmias and cold, ischemic fingers and toes.

nodes.label: Mitral TEER
nodes.summary: Transcatheter edge-to-edge repair clips the mitral leaflets together, through a venous catheter that crosses the atrial septum, to reduce the leak.

levers.why: Less regurgitant volume lowers left atrial and LV filling pressures.

nursingPriorities: Check the femoral venous access site for bleeding.
Report a new or louder murmur or worsening dyspnea, which can signal residual MR or a detached clip.

nodes.label: Mitral valve surgery
nodes.summary: Surgical repair or replacement of the mitral valve on cardiopulmonary bypass. It is the definitive treatment for papillary muscle rupture.

levers.why: A competent valve ends the regurgitant volume, lowering filling pressures.

nursingPriorities: Provide post-cardiac surgery care: bleeding, signs of tamponade, rhythm and pacing wires.
A mechanical valve needs lifelong warfarin; teach INR monitoring and bleeding precautions.

nodes.label: PCI
nodes.summary: Percutaneous coronary intervention opens a blocked coronary artery with a balloon and stent. In shock after acute MI, emergency revascularization of the culprit artery improves survival.

levers.why: Reopening the artery restores blood flow to ischemic muscle.

nursingPriorities: Check the radial or femoral access site and distal pulses.
Report recurrent chest pain or new ST changes, which may mean stent thrombosis.
Teach antiplatelet adherence; stopping early raises the risk of stent thrombosis.

nodes.label: SAVR
nodes.summary: Surgical aortic valve replacement on cardiopulmonary bypass, using a mechanical or biological valve.

levers.why: Removing the outflow obstruction lowers the pressure the LV must generate.

nursingPriorities: Provide post-cardiac surgery care: bleeding, signs of tamponade, rhythm (atrial fibrillation is common) and pacing wires.
A mechanical valve needs lifelong warfarin; teach INR monitoring and bleeding precautions.

nodes.label: TAVR
nodes.summary: Transcatheter aortic valve replacement: a collapsible valve is delivered by catheter, most often through the femoral artery, and expanded inside the diseased valve.

levers.why: Removing the outflow obstruction lowers the pressure the LV must generate.

nursingPriorities: Check the access site and distal pulses for bleeding, hematoma or limb ischemia.
Watch telemetry for new heart block; the valve sits near the conduction system and some patients need a pacemaker.
Do neuro checks for stroke after the procedure.

nodes.label: Intra-aortic balloon pump
nodes.summary: A balloon in the descending thoracic aorta inflates in diastole and deflates just before systole. Routine use in MI-related shock did not lower mortality in the IABP-SHOCK II trial, so it is used selectively.

levers.why: Diastolic inflation raises aortic diastolic pressure and coronary perfusion.
Deflation just before systole lowers the pressure the LV ejects against.
Lower afterload means less LV work.

nursingPriorities: Check timing on the arterial waveform: inflation at the dicrotic notch, deflation just before the next upstroke.
Keep the cannulated leg straight and check distal pulses; check the left radial pulse and urine output, because a migrating balloon can block the left subclavian or renal arteries.

nodes.label: Impella
nodes.summary: A microaxial flow pump placed across the aortic valve, most often from the femoral artery. It pulls blood from the LV and ejects it into the ascending aorta.

levers.why: Unloading the LV lowers wall stress and oxygen demand.
Continuous drainage lowers LV volume and filling pressure.

nursingPriorities: Watch for hemolysis (dark or red urine, rising LDH and free hemoglobin) and limb ischemia.
Report position and suction alarms; pump position is checked by echo.
Check the access leg and distal pulses.

nodes.label: VA-ECMO
nodes.summary: Venoarterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation drains venous blood, oxygenates it and returns it to the arterial system, supporting both heart and lungs.

levers.why: Retrograde flow into the aorta raises the pressure the LV must eject against, which can distend the LV.

nursingPriorities: Watch for LV distension, such as loss of arterial pulsatility and pulmonary edema; an LV vent such as an Impella may be added.
With femoral cannulation, check right radial SpO2 or ABG for differential hypoxemia.
Check perfusion of the cannulated limb and monitor bleeding and anticoagulation.
